task.description: RE-VALIDATION (rework attempt 1 of 3) of TEST-DESIGNER's claimed fix (commit 73b30ab) to the prior FAIL: AC3's test previously asserted a hardcoded pre-call count of 0 for designer-user's JIT-provisioned row, deterministically failing on any run after the first against the persistent bpm-default fixture. The claimed fix replaced the hardcoded 0 with a captured count_before baseline, asserting count_before+1 after call 1 and still count_before+1 after call 2. Independently open and read the actual AC3 test code (not the description) to confirm: (1) no hardcoded absolute count remains; (2) the baseline is captured before the first call, same query/scope as the post-call counts; (3) the test would still catch broken/duplicated provisioning, not a tautology; (4) test/specs/REQ-134.md's AC3 section matches the code. Then re-run the full 5-check list (a-e) from scratch on the whole file set, with particular attention to whether the AC3 fix actually eliminates the cross-invocation pollution risk or merely moves it.
acceptance_criteria: a test obtains a genuine token from the running Keycloak and drives it through Letflow.Plugs.AuthPipeline end to end, with the real assertion output quoted
the token's signature is verified against the live JWKS via the real verifier, not TokenVerifierDouble -- demonstrated by the test failing if pointed at a tampered token
JIT provisioning creates a real user row on first authentication and reuses it on the second, asserted across two calls
the default mix test run still passes with Keycloak stopped, quoted as evidence
the real-token tests skip with a message naming exactly what must be running, rather than failing obscurely
the result states the exact command a developer runs to execute them

result.summary:
Independently re-read test/specs/REQ-134.md, test/letflow/integration/keycloak_auth_pipeline_test.exs, test/support/keycloak_test_client.ex, test/test_helper.exs in full (fresh read, not trusting the prior gate's or TEST-DESIGNER's claims). AC1/AC2/AC6: unchanged from the prior pass, re-confirmed -- real coverage, no TODOs, no @tag :skip, no hardcoded secrets beyond the already-vetted seeded Keycloak dev credentials (admin-user/admin-pass, designer-user/designer-pass; grepped for 'password|secret|pass' across the three files, every hit is one of these two known seed creds or the literal string 'password' inside a form-encoding key name). AC4 re-confirmed myself this run: `docker compose ps` shows only postgres Up, then ran `mix test test/letflow/integration/keycloak_auth_pipeline_test.exs` -> 'Excluding tags: [:keycloak]' / 'Result: 0 tests, 3 excluded'. AC5: not re-derived (per task instructions, already independently probed and ruled compliant in the prior gate via direct ExUnit probing against this repo's installed 1.20.3 toolchain) -- no new evidence found that would contradict that ruling, so it stands. No 'TODO: implement test' anywhere in the file set.

AC3's claimed fix does NOT eliminate the defect the prior FAIL identified -- it moves it to a different assertion that fails under the exact same cross-invocation scenario. Traced this by reading the actual production code the test exercises, not by trusting the spec's own justification: lib/letflow/identity.ex's provision_oidc_user/4 -> upsert_by_external_identity/4 (line 1278) is a genuine find-or-create keyed on (tenant_id, external_realm, external_id) -- upsert_by_external_identity calls get_by_external_identity first and returns the EXISTING row with created: false if one matches, only calling insert_or_fetch (a Repo.insert with on_conflict: :nothing) when none is found. Combined with design section 5's own documented fact (restated correctly in the new moduledoc/spec) that the bpm-default tenant/schema, and therefore any User row JIT-provisioned inside it, is NEVER torn down between suite invocations, and that designer-user is a fixed seeded Keycloak identity whose JWT 'sub' claim is stable across every token mint (same underlying Keycloak user id every time -- verified by reading keycloak_test_client.ex's direct_access_token/4, which performs a plain resource-owner-password grant against the same seeded account, not a per-call-unique identity): on the database's FIRST-EVER run of this suite, count_before=0, call 1 creates the row (count_before+1=1, correct), call 2 reuses it (still 1, correct) -- this run passes. On the SECOND invocation of the exact command AC6/the spec documents (mix test --include keycloak test/letflow/integration/keycloak_auth_pipeline_test.exs) against that same, never-reset database, designer-user's row from the first invocation is still present when this test starts. count_before is captured at 1 (the pre-existing row). Call 1 now hits upsert_by_external_identity's EXISTING-row branch (get_by_external_identity finds the row created in run 1) and returns it unchanged -- no new row is inserted, because that is exactly what JIT provisioning is supposed to do for an identity it has already provisioned. The actual post-call-1 count therefore stays at 1 = count_before, not count_before + 1. `assert user_count_for_subject(schema_name, subject) == count_before + 1` (keycloak_auth_pipeline_test.exs line 265) fails deterministically on this second invocation. This is the identical failure class the prior gate blocked on (a fixture keyed to a shared, never-reset, hardcoded identity causing a cross-invocation assertion failure) -- the fix changed which line fails and on which invocation, but the suite is still certainly not repeatable across the exact command AC6 documents as normal usage. Note for the record: the prior gate's own suggested option (b) ('assert count_before, count_before+1, count_before+1') carried this same latent assumption -- that the first call within any given test invocation always performs a genuine first-time provision -- which is false given the permanent fixture plus find-or-create upsert semantics; TEST-DESIGNER implemented that suggestion faithfully, so this is a defect in the suggested remedy, not a deviation from it, and does not fault TEST-DESIGNER for following it.

The fix that actually restores repeatability is closer to the prior gate's option (a): the test (or its setup, once `subject` is known) must reset the row count for THIS subject to a true, invocation-independent zero before asserting anything -- e.g. `Repo.delete_all(from(u in User, where: u.external_realm == @realm and u.external_id == ^subject), prefix: schema_name)` immediately after computing `subject` and before capturing any count -- so `count_before` is provably 0 on every invocation, not merely 'whatever the database happens to hold going in'. A baseline captured without first clearing prior state is not a fix for a fixture that persists across invocations; it only defers the check the fixture violates to a spot the earlier hardcoded-0 test didn't reach on a first run.

Did not need to re-derive the tautology question in the abstract (check (3) from the task): with a correct reset-to-zero baseline, the assertions would still genuinely distinguish broken provisioning (count stays at 0, caught) from non-reuse on the second call (count reaches 2, caught) from correct behavior (0 -> 1 -> 1) -- the test's shape is sound, only its baseline-acquisition step is broken.

issues.description: test/letflow/integration/keycloak_auth_pipeline_test.exs AC3 test ('first call provisions a user row, second call reuses it', line 241-273): the count_before baseline is captured from live database state without first resetting it, so on the SECOND and every subsequent invocation of the exact command AC6 documents (mix test --include keycloak ... against the same persistent letflow_test database), designer-user's JIT-provisioned row from a PRIOR invocation is already present when count_before is captured. lib/letflow/identity.ex's upsert_by_external_identity/4 (called via provision_oidc_user/4) is a genuine find-or-create keyed on (tenant_id, external_realm, external_id) -- confirmed by reading the code -- so call 1 on that second invocation finds the existing row and does NOT insert a new one. The actual post-call-1 count stays at count_before, not count_before + 1, so `assert user_count_for_subject(schema_name, subject) == count_before + 1` (line 265) fails deterministically. Rework required: reset this subject's row count to a true zero before capturing any baseline -- e.g. delete any existing User row matching (external_realm: "bpm-default", external_id: <designer-user's sub>) in that schema immediately after deriving `subject`, before computing count_before -- so the test is correct on every invocation, not just the database's first-ever one. Reflect the corrected mechanism in test/specs/REQ-134.md's AC3 section (its current 'why a baseline count' justification is itself incomplete -- it explains why a hardcoded 0 was wrong but does not address that an un-reset baseline has the same defect one invocation later).

result.next_action: Rework TEST-DESIGNER -- fix AC3's still-unresolved cross-invocation repeatability defect (BLOCKER above), rework iteration 2 of 3. AC1/AC2/AC4/AC5/AC6 and checks (a)/(b)/(e) all PASS and do not need to be revisited; only the AC3 baseline-reset mechanism needs rework.

gate_history.summary: AC1/AC2/AC6 pass; AC4 and AC5 independently re-verified and AC5's raise-vs-skip deviation ruled compliant. BLOCKER found under checks (c)/(d): AC3's test asserted a hardcoded pre-call count of 0 for designer-user's JIT-provisioned row, but the bpm-default tenant/schema (and any row provisioned in it) is never torn down between invocations (design section 5), and designer-user is a fixed seeded Keycloak identity with no per-run uniqueness available -- so the test passes on a database's first-ever run and fails deterministically on every subsequent run of AC6's own documented command.
issues: BLOCKER: AC3's hardcoded pre-call count of 0 is not repeatable across invocations of the same persistent test database; rework required via either (a) an on_exit/teardown deleting the JIT-provisioned row after the test, or (b) a count captured before either pipeline call as a baseline, asserted as count_before/count_before+1/count_before+1.
